--- title: "Guide for Reproducible Research" subtitle: "What do we mean by reproducible?" format: stat159slides-revealjs chalkboard: true --- # Guide for Reproducible Research ## Reading ::: {.nonincremental} - Chapter: **Guide for Reproducible Research** - Book: The Turing Way - Year: 2024 - ::: # Reproducibility ## {.nostretch} ![](images/reproduction-replica-cartoon.png){width=70% fig-align="center"} ## What is the right verb? . . . ![](images/what-is-the-right-verb.svg){width=70% fig-align="center"} ## The Turing Way 2x2 Matrix \ ``` [ SAME DATA ] [ DIFFERENT DATA ] ┌───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐ [ SAME │ │ │ ANALYSIS]│ │ │ ├───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤ [ DIFF. │ │ │ ANALYSIS]│ │ │ └───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘ ``` ## The Turing Way 2x2 Matrix \ ``` [ SAME DATA ] [ DIFFERENT DATA ] ┌───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐ [ SAME │ REPRODUCIBLE │ │ ANALYSIS]│ (Same steps & data) │ │ ├───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤ [ DIFF. │ │ │ ANALYSIS]│ │ │ └───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘ ``` ## The Turing Way 2x2 Matrix \ ``` [ SAME DATA ] [ DIFFERENT DATA ] ┌───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐ [ SAME │ REPRODUCIBLE │ │ ANALYSIS]│ (Same steps & data) │ │ ├───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤ [ DIFF. │ ROBUST │ │ ANALYSIS]│ (Language agnostic) │ │ └───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘ ``` ## The Turing Way 2x2 Matrix \ ``` [ SAME DATA ] [ DIFFERENT DATA ] ┌───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐ [ SAME │ REPRODUCIBLE │ REPLICABLE │ ANALYSIS]│ (Same steps & data) │ (Qualitately similar) │ ├───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤ [ DIFF. │ ROBUST │ │ ANALYSIS]│ (Language agnostic) │ │ └───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘ ``` ## The Turing Way 2x2 Matrix \ ``` [ SAME DATA ] [ DIFFERENT DATA ] ┌───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐ [ SAME │ REPRODUCIBLE │ REPLICABLE │ ANALYSIS]│ (Same steps & data) │ (Qualitately similar) │ ├───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤ [ DIFF. │ ROBUST │ GENERALISABLE │ ANALYSIS]│ (Language agnostic) │ (The Holy Grail) │ └───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘ ``` . . . ::: {.callout-note} ### Takeaway Computational reproducibility specifically requires obtaining the **same results** using the **same data** and **same code/analysis**. ::: ::: {.notes} - Point out that terms like "reproducible" and "replicable" are often used interchangeably in lay conversations, but *The Turing Way* establishes precise definitions along a 2x2 grid. - Walk through each quadrant: - **Reproducible**: Same data + Same code. This is our baseline standard in computational data science. - **Replicable**: Different data + Same pipeline. Tests if the finding holds up in a new sample or dataset. - **Robust**: Same data + Different pipeline. Tests if the finding is an artifact of a specific software package, model choice, or script. - **Generalisable**: Different data + Different pipeline. The gold standard for scientific claims. - Remind students: In this course, we focus heavily on the top-left quadrant (Reproducibility) as the foundation for all the others. ::: ## Reproducible $\neq$ Open Data - **Open Science** promotes making data, code, and papers freely available to everyone. - **Computational Reproducibility** focuses on code execution logic, pipeline integrity, and environment preservation. - A project with restricted or sensitive data (e.g., medical, commercial) can still be **fully reproducible** through: - Synthetic test datasets. - Containerized environments (Docker). - Secure, audited execution pipelines. ::: {.notes} - Address a common student misconception: "My dataset has human subjects / proprietary business data, so I can't make my project reproducible." - Clarify that *Open* and *Reproducible* overlap, but are distinct concepts. - Explain how to make restricted data projects reproducible: 1. Provide synthetic or scrambled mock data that mirrors the schema so external users can verify the code runs. 2. Write deterministic unit tests and containerize the environment. 3. Ensure that an authorized auditor inside a secure enclave could re-run the exact script and get identical results. ::: ## Reproducibility as "Personal Insurance" Working reproducibly benefits **you** (and your team) first: - [Future-proofing:]{.bold-hilit} Your primary collaborator six months from now is *your future self*. - [Seamless onboarding:]{.bold-hilit} New lab members can run existing pipelines without months of reconstruction. - [Error resilience:]{.bold-hilit} Automated pipelines make updating figures or fixing small bugs fast and low-risk. ::: {.notes} - Frame reproducibility not as an altruistic duty for science, but as self-preservation. - Ask the class: "Have you ever opened a project you worked on 6 months ago and spent 2 hours trying to remember which script to run first?" - Emphasize "Your future self doesn't reply to emails." If you don't document relative paths, dependencies, and execution order today, your future self will suffer. - Mention that automated pipelines (like Make or `targets` in R) allow you to re-render an entire 50-page manuscript or dashboard with one command after updating raw data. ::: ## The "Added Advantage": Credit & Citation Publishing reproducible workflows directly boosts academic impact: - [Higher Citations:]{.bold-hilit} Papers with public code and data receive demonstrably higher citation rates. - [Greater Trust:]{.bold-hilit} Independent researchers can audit, verify, and build directly on your work. - [Secondary Outputs:]{.bold-hilit} Reusable R packages, Python libraries, and pipelines earn recognition as first-class scientific contributions. ::: {.notes} - Highlight the selfish incentives for doing open/reproducible work: literature consistently shows a "citation advantage" for papers with publicly available code and data repositories. - Explain that code repositories (GitHub/Zenodo with DOIs) allow other researchers to cite your *tools* even if they aren't citing your specific empirical findings. - Trust is currency in science: when readers can inspect your raw scripts and computational pipeline, they treat your findings with far higher confidence. ::: ## Barrier: The "Career Tax" & Incentive Gap - [Publication Bias:]{.bold-hilit} Academic hiring, tenure, and grants overwhelmingly reward *novel findings* over robust software engineering or replication studies. - [The Time Sink:]{.bold-hilit} Documenting code, setting up continuous integration, and containerizing environments takes significant time. - [Incentive Gap:]{.bold-hilit} Without institutional rewards, researchers view reproducible practices as an unrewarded **"career tax."** ::: {.notes} - Connect this to real-world career incentives (hiring, tenure, grant funding). - Point out the tension: Building a clean, modular, fully tested pipeline takes 2-3x longer than writing a quick "one-off" messy script. - If hiring committees only count the *number* of novel publications on a resume, the researcher who takes shortcuts will publish faster than the researcher who builds reproducible infrastructure. - Ask the class: "How do we fix this incentive structure in data science and computational fields?" ::: ## Barrier: Resource & Infrastructure Deficits Reproducibility requires resources that are often underfunded or unevenly distributed: - [Skills Gap:]{.bold-hilit} Training in software engineering (Git, virtual environments, pipelines) is rarely built into scientific curricula. - [Compute Costs:]{.bold-hilit} Heavy computational pipelines (e.g., multi-GPU training) can be financially prohibitive to re-run or audit. - [Maintenance:]{.bold-hilit} Software dependencies drift over time, requiring continuous maintenance to stay executable. ::: {.notes} - Summarize the physical and structural resource barriers: 1. **Knowledge gap**: Most domain scientists were never formally taught Git, Docker, or environment isolation—they are self-taught out of necessity. 2. **Financial/Compute gap**: Re-running a deep learning model or climate simulation might cost thousands of dollars in cloud computing credits. 3. **Dependency drift**: R packages and Python libraries update constantly. A script written in 2020 may fail in 2026 if packages aren't pinned (`renv`/`uv`/`conda`). - Conclude by setting up the transition to the next part of your course: teaching the practical tools (Git, Quarto, environments) that help overcome these exact barriers. ::: # Discussion Time ## Screens Off, Minds On \ ::: {.nonincremental} - [Devices Away:]{.bold-hilit} Laptops & tablets closed, phones away. - [No One Alone:]{.bold-hilit} Pair or team up (no solo seats). - [Engage Fully:]{.bold-hilit} Be ready to speak, debate, and share ideas. ::: ## Scenario A Two candidates are competing for a single tenure-track position: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} [Candidate A publishes 5 papers a year]{.mdlit}. Their code is undocumented, scattered across local desktop folders, and missing computational environments, but their results are novel and published in high-impact venues. ::: ::: {.column width="5%"} ::: ::: {.column width="45%" .fragment} [Candidate B publishes 2 papers a year]{.hilit}. Every project features fully documented Quarto/Jupyter workflows, continuous integration tests, archived Docker containers on Zenodo, and granular version control. ::: :::: . . . \ The hiring committee selects Candidate A, citing their superior _"publication volume and research productivity."_ ## Scenario A (cont'd) \ ::: {.poll} What changes in hiring/granting committees would level the playing field for [Candidate B]{.hilit}? ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
03:00
``` ::: ::: ## Scenario B A team of data science undergraduates is building a data pipeline for their capstone project. They have 4 weeks remaining. They can either: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="46%"} [Option 1:]{.mdlit} Spend the final 4 weeks expanding their modeling techniques, exploring two new algorithms, and refining their presentation figures. ::: ::: {.column width="5%"} ::: ::: {.column width="46%" .fragment} [Option 2:]{.hilit} Spend the final 4 weeks refactoring code into modular packages, writing unit tests, capturing software dependencies, and setting up automated pipelines. ::: :::: . . . ::: {.poll} What option would you choose (and why)? ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
03:00
``` ::: ::: ## Scenario C A research group in climate modeling trains a deep learning architecture for 6 days across a cluster of 32 GPUs, costing $15,000 in cloud compute credits. A peer reviewer asks the team to re-run the entire pipeline with three alternative random seed initializations to prove statistical stability. The group's grant budget is exhausted, and their compute allocation has expired. . . . ::: {.poll} Draft a _reproducibility rescue plan_ detailing 3 specific strategies they can provide to peer reviewers to prove their pipeline is trustworthy. ::: ::: {.notes} 1) Intermediate State Archiving: Saving and publishing model checkpoints, raw log outputs, and loss curves on repositories like Zenodo/OSF. 2) Dry-Run / Toy Pipelines: Providing a fast, low-compute "mock" version of the pipeline using a small synthetic dataset so others can verify the code logic end-to-end in seconds. 3) Deterministic Sub-sampling: Demonstrating stability on a lightweight, representative subset of the data before scaling up to full GPU clusters. 4) Environment & Seed Logging: Strictly archiving the exact container image (Docker), fixed random seeds, and hardware specs so that even if others can't run it now, the execution state is perfectly preserved for the future. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
03:00
``` ::: ::: # Quiz-Poll Time Open your laptops / phones ## Google Form \ ![](images/poll-02-qr-code.svg){fig-align="center"} \ [tinyurl.com/3b2fmasf](https://tinyurl.com/3b2fmasf) # Bonus Take Aways ## > "A study can be reproducible and still be wrong." > > Roger Peng, 2014 . . . \ > "Just because a result is reproducible does not make it right, > and just because it is not reproducible does not make it wrong." > > Nature

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
